lessons.0.title: Professional Tasting Terminology
lessons.0.slides.0.title: Professional Tasting Terminology
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 1 - 19 min
lessons.0.slides.0.description: Building a professional wine-tasting vocabulary from scratch
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Why Does Tasting Terminology Matter?
lessons.0.slides.1.content: **From Subjective Feeling to Objective Description** — A great tasting note is not 'this wine tastes good'. It is a precise, reproducible, objectively communicable record. Professional tasting terminology allows you to: communicate accurately (specialists worldwide use the same vocabulary); record reliably (notes can still be useful 10–20 years later); assess objectively (separate personal preference from quality evaluation); command authority (make buyers, sommeliers, and journalists trust your judgment). **International Standard Systems** — WSET (Wine & Spirit Education Trust): the most widely recognised international system with systematic SAT methodology. Court of Master Sommeliers (CMS): focused on the restaurant trade. Wine Spectator / Parker / Burghound: journalist scoring systems, each with its own vocabulary. French traditional: still commonly used in Burgundy itself. This module teaches WSET as the core, supplemented by terms commonly used by Burgundy specialists.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: Appearance — Clarity and Intensity
lessons.0.slides.2.content: **Clarity** (important for quality assessment): Brilliant: perfectly clear, no particles, glass-like transparency — standard for quality wine; Clear: clear with only trace particles; Dull: slight haziness, may be caused by natural protein or unfiltered wine (not necessarily a fault); Hazy: obvious cloudiness, usually a fault — may indicate refermentation in the bottle or bacterial contamination. **Colour Intensity**: Pale, medium, deep. **Colour by Grape and Age** (Pinot Noir): Young (0–3 yrs): deep purple, bright ruby, blue-tinged edges; Developing (3–8 yrs): garnet, slightly orange edges; Mature (8–15 yrs): brick red, amber edges; Old (15+ yrs): tawny, orange edges. **Chardonnay Color**: Young: straw yellow, lemon, slight green; Developing: gold; Mature: deep gold, amber; Old: amber (may be oxidised). **Observation Tips**: Tilt the glass against a white background under natural light; observe colour from the deepest part of the bowl to the edge (rim variation).
lessons.0.slides.3.title: Appearance Terminology Quick Reference
lessons.0.slides.4.title: Aromas — Three Levels of Classification
lessons.0.slides.4.content: **Primary Aromas (Varietal)** — Direct from the grape variety itself: Red fruits (young Pinot Noir): strawberry, raspberry, cherry, cranberry; Black fruits (mature/Grand Cru Pinot): blackberry, black cherry, black plum, blackcurrant; Floral: violet, rose, peony (typical Chambolle-Musigny); Herbal: tea leaves, mint, green pepper (cool-climate characteristic); Earthy: forest floor, mushroom (mature Côte de Nuits). **Secondary Aromas (Fermentation)** — From fermentation processes: Yeast: bread, yeast, biscuit (more typical of white wines); MLF (malolactic fermentation): butter, cream, diacetyl (Chardonnay characteristic); Red berries after fermentation: intensified cherry, jam notes. **Tertiary Aromas (Maturation)** — From maturation and ageing: Oak (new barrels): vanilla, coconut, toast, cedar, smoke; Bottle ageing: forest floor/sous-bois (mature Burgundy hallmark), leather, cigar box, tobacco, game, earth; Umami: soy sauce, mushroom (very mature Pinot Noir); Animal: game, musk, barnyard (specific domaines); Dried fruit: dried plum, fig, raisin (very old wines). **Aromatic Intensity**: Low, medium, medium-plus, high.
lessons.0.slides.5.title: Aroma Wheel — Burgundy Pinot Noir
lessons.0.slides.6.title: Palate — The Complete Vocabulary
lessons.0.slides.6.content: **The Seven Core Palate Components**: 1️⃣ **Sweetness** (even in dry wine): Bone dry, dry, off-dry, medium, medium-sweet, sweet, luscious — Burgundy Grand Cru is typically dry but may have a trace of sweetness from very ripe fruit. 2️⃣ **Acidity**: Flabby (low), low, medium, medium-plus, high, very high — Burgundy Pinot Noir is typically medium to medium-plus; Chablis white can be high. 3️⃣ **Tannin** (red wine): Low, medium, medium-plus, high, very high; Texture: green/hard (unripe), firm (structure), ripe (mature), soft (velvet), silky (premium). 4️⃣ **Alcohol**: Low (<11%), medium (11–13%), medium-high (13–14%), high (>14%); New climate years (2020, 2022) can reach 14.5%+. 5️⃣ **Body**: Light, medium, medium-full, full — Chambolle tends to lighter; Gevrey to fuller. 6️⃣ **Texture**: Watery, thin, lean, structured, rich, viscous, creamy (white), grippy. 7️⃣ **Finish**: Short (<5 sec), medium (5–10 sec), long (10–30 sec), very long (>30 sec); Exceptional Grand Cru can reach 40–60+ seconds; Flavour evolution on the finish.
lessons.0.slides.7.title: Structure and Complexity — Advanced Vocabulary
lessons.0.slides.7.content: **Structure** — The framework that holds a wine together: Balance (the most important concept): all components are in harmony — no single element is dominant; Integration: oak, tannin, acid, and fruit have merged seamlessly; Grip: the tactile sensation of tannin (can be fine-grained or coarse); Length: how long the wine persists on the palate after swallowing. **Complexity** — The richness and layering of flavour: Simple: a single primary fruit note; Moderate: two to three flavour notes; Complex: multiple layers simultaneously (fruit + earth + spice + minerals); Profound: evolving, changing, revealing deeper dimensions over time. **Special Burgundy Terminology**: Typicité: how faithfully the wine represents its terroir character; Élégance: elegance — the signature of premium Burgundy; Minéralité: minerality — the chalky, slate-like sensation from Chablis or limestone terroir; Précision: aromatic precision, clean, clearly defined; Tension: the interplay of high acidity and ripe fruit; Transparence: the degree to which the wine expresses its terroir. **Quality Levels (WSET)**: Faulty → Poor → Acceptable → Good → Very Good → Outstanding
lessons.0.slides.8.title: Tasting Terminology — Common Mistakes and Corrections
lessons.0.slides.8.points.0: ❌ 'Smells like wine' → ✅ 'Aromas of ripe cherry and dried rose petals'
lessons.0.slides.8.points.2: ❌ 'A bit dry' → ✅ 'Tannins are firm, slightly grippy, need 5+ years'
lessons.0.slides.8.points.3: ❌ 'A little sour' → ✅ 'High acidity, refreshing, lends to excellent ageing potential'
lessons.0.slides.8.points.4: ❌ 'Good colour' → ✅ 'Deep ruby with garnet edges; clear and brilliant'
lessons.0.slides.8.points.5: ❌ 'A bit harsh' → ✅ 'Firm, ripe tannins that will soften with 10 years of cellaring'
lessons.0.slides.8.points.6: ❌ 'Tastes like Burgundy' → ✅ 'Classic Côte de Nuits: forest floor, ripe cherry, fine-grained tannin, long finish'
lessons.0.slides.8.points.7: ❌ 'It has a smell' → ✅ 'Tertiary aromas: forest floor, mushroom, cigar box'

lessons.1.title: Comparing Scoring Systems
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Comparing Scoring Systems
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 19 min
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Understanding the major wine scoring systems and their influence
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Why Do Scoring Systems Matter?
lessons.1.slides.1.content: **Scoring is the currency of the wine world** — A single point can change a wine's market price by tens of thousands of NT dollars. Understanding scoring systems helps you: interpret wine scores correctly; see through marketing copy; make rational buying decisions; understand price formation mechanisms. **The Influence of Scoring Systems on Prices**: Parker 95+ score → typical price increase of 50–100 %; Burghound 94+ → top Burgundy; JR 17+ → premium recommendation; Decanter Platinum → international visibility. **Important Caveat**: Scores are subjective assessments by individual reviewers. Different systems have different scales, biases, and emphases. Scores are a reference tool, not an absolute truth. Learn to cross-reference and develop your own judgment.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: Robert Parker / Wine Advocate — The 100-Point System
lessons.1.slides.2.content: **Background**: Robert Parker (RP) published The Wine Advocate from 1978; his 100-point system became the global industry standard. The Wine Advocate today is owned by a Singapore investment group; Neal Martin covers Burgundy. **Scale**: 50–59 Unacceptable; 60–69 Below average; 70–79 Average; 80–84 Good; 85–89 Very good; 90–95 Outstanding; 96–100 Extraordinary. **Key Characteristics** — Burgundy focus: Neal Martin and William Kelley are current reviewers; they have a stronger preference for texture, ripeness, and concentration than Parker did. Publication: both online and print; subscription-based. Influence: Parker-era Bordeaux bias; influence on Burgundy is declining, but very mature references still use his scores. **Score interpretation**: 90–92 = great price-to-quality ratio; 93–95 = top quality for investment; 96–100 = collectors' targets — expect 100 %+ price premium. **Note**: Parker's personal taste leaned towards big, concentrated styles; Burgundy lovers should cross-reference with Burghound.
lessons.1.slides.3.title: Burghound — The Burgundy Bible
lessons.1.slides.3.content: **Background**: Allen Meadows (alias Burghound) launched Burghound.com in 2000 and is recognized as the world's foremost Burgundy authority. **Key Facts**: Published 4× per year; covers every Burgundy appellation in-depth; subscription: $125/year (considered essential by serious collectors). **Scale**: 80–100 points with ultra-precise standards; 88–90: very good, good everyday drinking; 91–93: excellent, investment consideration; 94–95: outstanding, high priority; 96–98: profound, rare; **99–100: almost never awarded (reserved for once-in-a-lifetime wines)**. **Why Burghound?** His in-depth knowledge of Burgundy is unmatched; he visits nearly every producer in person; he has long-term tracking going back 20+ years; his assessments are highly consistent. **Price Impact**: Burghound 96+ = immediately sold out for allocation wine. **Reading Burghound Notes**: He typically identifies: precision, translucency, typicité (whether the wine expresses its terroir), tension, minerality; he tends to be more conservative than Parker.
lessons.1.slides.4.title: Jancis Robinson — The 20-Point British System
lessons.1.slides.4.content: **Background**: Jancis Robinson MW (Master of Wine) is one of the UK's top critics and a member of the Queen's royal household. She runs JancisRobinson.com. **Scale**: 12 = Faulty or undrinkable; 13 = Unacceptable; 14 = Acceptable; 15 = Acceptable to good; 16 = Good, recommended; 17 = Distinguished, outstanding; 17.5 = Very distinguished; 18 = Excellent; 18.5 = Elite; 19 = Exceptional; 20 = Perfect (almost never). **Key Characteristics**: A 20-pt score ≈ a 100-pt score: 16/20 = ~87–89; 17/20 = ~90–92; 18/20 = ~93–95; 19/20 = ~96–99. More conservative than Parker; preferred by the British market and traditional European producers. JancisRobinson.com covers Burgundy very comprehensively; often reviews the same wines as Burghound, enabling comparison. **Strengths**: Objective, does not court producers, respects traditional Burgundy elegance.
lessons.1.slides.5.title: Comparing Major Scoring Systems
lessons.1.slides.6.title: Other Key Critics and Platforms
lessons.1.slides.6.content: **Antonio Galloni / Vinous** (vinous.com, $165/yr): Formerly at The Wine Advocate; launched Vinous in 2013; strong on Burgundy, Barolo, Champagne; 100-pt scale similar to Parker; generally consistent with Burghound (slight luxury/concentration bias). **Decanter** (decanter.com): 5-star system: 1★ Faulty; 2★ Poor; 3★ Recommended; 4★ Highly Recommended; 5★ (Platinum) Outstanding; a 5-star award is an international visibility boost. **Wine Spectator** (WineSpectator.com): 100-pt; the most-read American wine magazine; broad coverage; Burgundy specialisation less deep than Burghound; Annual Top 100 list is hugely influential. **James Suckling** (JamesSuckling.com): 100-pt; fast, prolific; slightly more generous scoring; Bordeaux and Italian wine focus; Burgundy less authoritative. **La Revue du Vin de France (RVF)**: The oldest and most authoritative French magazine; 20-pt; rarely gives 20/20; highly respected by French producers; a valuable supplement for traditional-style Burgundy.
lessons.1.slides.7.title: Score-to-Price Impact Analysis
lessons.1.slides.7.content: **How Scores Move Markets** (real examples): 2015 DRC Romanée-Conti: Parker 100, Burghound 99, JR 20 → price went from €15,000 (2016 futures) to €30,000+ (2020 market); 2015 Rousseau Chambertin: Parker 98, Burghound 97 → wholesale doubled; 2010 DRC La Tâche: Parker 99, Burghound 98 → auction average 200 % above release price. **Score Premium Formula** (approximate): Parker/Vinous 90–92: no premium; 93–95: +20–40 %; 96–98: +80–150 %; 99–100: +200–500 %. Burghound 91–93: +10–20 %; 94–95: +30–60 %; 96–98: +80–200 %; 99+: priceless. **Limitations of Scoring**: Scores are snapshots at a single moment; a wine may score better or worse at different times. Critics have personal taste biases. Score inflation: overall scores trend upward year-on-year. **How to Use Scores Rationally**: Cross-reference 3+ critics; pay attention to tasting notes, not just the number; understand each critic's style (Parker likes big; JR likes elegant); develop your own scoring ability.

lessons.2.title: Structure of Tasting Notes
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Structure of Tasting Notes
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 19 min
lessons.2.slides.1.title: Tasting Note Methodology — WSET SAT
lessons.2.slides.1.content: **WSET Systematic Approach to Tasting (SAT)** — A standardised, globally recognised evaluation framework: **Appearance (Sight)**: Clarity (brilliant/clear/dull/hazy); Intensity (pale/medium/deep); Colour; Other observations (bubbles, legs/tears). **Nose (Smell)**: Condition (clean/faulty — TCA, oxidation, VA); Intensity (light/medium/aromatic/pronounced); Aroma characteristics (primary/secondary/tertiary); Development (youthful/developing/mature/tired). **Palate (Taste)**: Sweetness; Acidity; Tannin (red wine); Alcohol; Body; Texture; Flavour characteristics and intensity; Finish (short/medium/long/very long). **Conclusions**: Quality (faulty/poor/acceptable/good/very good/outstanding); Ageing potential; Likely ID (grape variety, appellation, vintage); Drinking window. **CMS Method (restaurant sommeliers)**: 4-step in 3–4 minutes — Sight → Nose → Palate → Conclusion; more concise, designed for professional table service; same components but more compact expression.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 📝 Complete Tasting Note Template
lessons.2.slides.2.content: **Header Information** — Wine name: [Producer] [Appellation] [Year]; Date: [Year, Month, Day]; Occasion: [Blind / Open / Vertical]; Decant: [How long]; Temperature: [°C]. **Appearance** — Clarity: [brilliant]; Intensity: [deep]; Colour: [ruby with garnet edges]. **Nose** — Condition: [clean]; Intensity: [pronounced]; Primary: [ripe cherry, wild strawberry, rose petal]; Secondary: [cream, subtle spice]; Tertiary: [forest floor, sous-bois, cigar box, dark earth]; Development: [mature]. **Palate** — Sweetness: [dry]; Acidity: [medium-plus]; Tannin: [medium, fine-grained, silky]; Alcohol: [medium, 13.5 %]; Body: [medium-full]; Texture: [velvet, creamy]; Flavour: [cherry, wild strawberry, mushroom, earth, dark spice]; Finish: [very long, 45+ sec]. **Conclusions** — Quality: [Outstanding]; Ageing: [holds well to 2035–2045]; Identity: [Côte de Nuits, Pinot Noir, premier or grand cru, 10–15 yr old]; Overall: [a complex, profound wine with typicité and élégance — classic Burgundy].
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 💎 Real-World Example — 2015 DRC La Tâche
lessons.2.slides.3.content: **Wine Information**: 2015 DRC (Domaine de la Romanée-Conti) La Tâche Grand Cru, 750 ml; Opened for 90 minutes; Served at 16°C. **Appearance**: Clear and brilliant; deep ruby with garnet edges; tears slow and wide — indicates high alcohol and glycerol. **Nose**: Absolutely clean, no faults; Pronounced intensity; Primary: ripe wild cherry, black plum, fresh raspberry, dark rose petals; Secondary: cream, very subtle spice (cinnamon); Tertiary: forest floor (sous-bois), earth, smoke, tea leaves, dark earth; Development: mature, complex layering. **Palate**: Dry; Acidity: medium-plus — lively and refreshing; Tannin: medium — silky, incredibly fine-grained, no astringency; Alcohol: medium-high (~14 %, well-integrated, warm but not hot); Body: medium-full; Texture: velvet, pure, smooth as liquid silk; Flavour: cherry, dark plum, mushroom, earth, smoke, dark spice, tea; Finish: very long, 50+ seconds, evolving in waves. **Conclusions**: Quality: Outstanding — arguably 'Profound'; Age: holds to 2045+; optimal drinking 2028–2040; Identity: this is unmistakably La Tâche — unique among all Grand Crus; Overall Score: 96–98/100; this is what 'greatness' in Burgundy means.
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Choosing Your Tasting Note Tool
lessons.2.slides.5.title: ✍️ 10 Tips for Professional Tasting Notes
lessons.2.slides.5.points.0: 1. Be specific, not vague: 'wild cherry' over 'red fruit'; 'dark earth' over 'earthy'
lessons.2.slides.5.points.1: 2. Use a clear structure: Appearance → Nose → Palate → Conclusions, always in the same order
lessons.2.slides.5.points.2: 3. Be objective: separate quality assessment from personal preference
lessons.2.slides.5.points.4: 5. Avoid clichés: overuse of 'elegant', 'complex', 'balanced' without explanation
lessons.2.slides.5.points.5: 6. Record context: temperature, decant time, occasion, glass type — all affect perception
lessons.2.slides.5.points.6: 7. Note evolution: how the wine changes in the glass and with time
lessons.2.slides.5.points.7: 8. Include a drinking recommendation: now / hold X years / past peak
lessons.2.slides.5.points.8: 9. Score after the notes: don't let the score bias your evaluation
lessons.2.slides.5.points.9: 10. Review: re-read notes from 1–2 years ago to check predictions and improve
lessons.2.slides.6.title: Common Tasting Note Errors — Before and After
lessons.2.slides.7.title: The Art of Blind Tasting
lessons.2.slides.7.content: **Why Blind Taste?** — Eliminates label bias; sharpens observation skills; tests knowledge objectively. **Systematic Blind Tasting Framework** (WSET/CMS approach): Sight: colour depth, hue → estimate age and variety; Nose: primary aromas → variety/region; aromatic intensity → wine style; Palate: acid/tannin/body → region and vintage; structure → age-worthiness; **Conclusion (WSET approach)**: Country / Region / Vintage. **Burgundy Clues**: Ruby + garnet edge = aged Pinot Noir; Forest floor + cherry + silky tannin = Côte de Nuits; Pale + high acid + mineral = Chablis; Cream + hazelnut + pineapple = aged Côte de Beaune Chardonnay; High acid + lean body = cool vintage; Rich fruit + full body = warm vintage. **Practice Method**: Start with known wines, check yourself; then blind taste in groups; keep notes and compare predictions with actual wines; track improvement over time.

lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 18 min
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Applying professional skills: from village wine to Grand Cru to DRC
lessons.3.slides.1.title: Report 1 — Village Burgundy
lessons.3.slides.1.content: **Wine**: 2019 Louis Jadot Gevrey-Chambertin Village; Context: a business dinner; open 30 minutes; served at 15°C. **Appearance**: Clear and brilliant; medium ruby, slight garnet edge; medium-thick tears, slight legs. **Nose**: Clean, no faults; medium intensity; Primary: fresh cherry, red plum, raspberry; Secondary: slight cream and spice from French oak; Tertiary: a hint of forest floor; Development: youthful, still opening. **Palate**: Dry; Acidity: medium-plus, lively; Tannin: medium, slightly firm — will soften with 2–3 more years; Alcohol: medium (13 %); Body: medium; Texture: smooth but not yet silky; Flavour: cherry, red plum, vanilla, spice; Finish: medium, 8–10 seconds. **Conclusions**: Quality: Good to Very Good; Age: drink now to 2027; Identity: Gevrey Village level, classic Jadot style — reliable, well-crafted; Score: 88/100; **Comment**: An excellent representative of village-level Gevrey-Chambertin. Louis Jadot's expertise ensures consistent quality. At NT$3,500–4,500 it represents excellent price-to-quality. Best served with roast lamb or mushroom risotto.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: Report 2 — Grand Cru
lessons.3.slides.2.content: **Wine**: 2015 Domaine Armand Rousseau Chambertin Grand Cru; Context: a vertical tasting; open 120 minutes; served at 16°C. **Appearance**: Clear and brilliant; deep ruby with garnet edges; slow, wide tears — high alcohol and glycerol; the colour has deepened with 8 years of bottle age. **Nose**: Perfectly clean; Pronounced intensity; Primary: ripe black cherry, dark plum, dried roses, dark berries; Secondary: cream, a hint of fine French oak spice; Tertiary: forest floor (sous-bois), leather, tobacco, dark earth, dried herbs, mushroom; Development: mature, multi-layered, constantly evolving. **Palate**: Bone dry; Acidity: high, lively, perfectly structured; Tannin: medium-plus, ripe, incredibly fine-grained and silky — Chambertin's signature; Alcohol: medium-high (~14 %, fully integrated); Body: full; Texture: velvet, pure, seamless; Flavour: black cherry, tobacco, forest floor, mushroom, dark earth, dark spice; Finish: very long, 40+ seconds, flavours continue to evolve and emerge. **Conclusions**: Quality: Outstanding; Age: optimal 2025–2040, still has immense potential; Identity: Grand Cru Chambertin, pure Rousseau expression; Score: 96/100; **Comment**: This is the definition of Chambertin. Rousseau's meticulous farming and precision winemaking produce wines of extraordinary depth and elegance. Chambertin is the 'King of Burgundy' — this bottle demonstrates exactly why. Serve with roasted pigeon or aged Époisses cheese.
lessons.3.slides.3.title: Report 3 — DRC Level
lessons.3.slides.3.content: **Wine**: 2015 DRC Romanée-Conti Grand Cru; Context: special occasion tasting; open 3 hours; served at 17°C. **Appearance**: Clear and brilliant; deep, concentrated ruby with garnet edges; very slow, rich legs; the colour is remarkably vibrant for a 10-year-old wine. **Nose**: Flawless, unimpeachable; Extremely pronounced, multi-dimensional; Primary: wild cherry, black plum, dried rose petals, raspberry; Secondary: cream, subtle spice from 100 % new French oak (perfectly integrated, not apparent); Tertiary: forest floor, earth, cigar box, tobacco, dried herbs, sea spray, truffle, leather; Development: profound, evolving, revealing new dimensions every 10 minutes. **Palate**: Bone dry; Acidity: high yet perfectly balanced — lifts and refreshes; Tannin: very fine, gossamer-like, melts on the palate — like liquid silk; Alcohol: high (14.5 %, barely perceptible — fully integrated); Body: full, yet weightless; Texture: like liquid silk — there is no more perfect descriptor; Flavour: cherry, wild strawberry, truffle, dark earth, cigar, spice, sea minerals — all simultaneously; Finish: very long, 60+ seconds, flavours continue to transform after swallowing; a long, multi-wave crescendo. **Conclusions**: Quality: Outstanding — Profound; Age: optimal 2030–2055, nearly 30 years of potential; Identity: this is Romanée-Conti, unmistakable — there is nothing else like it; Score: 98–100/100; **Comment**: Romanée-Conti is the most discussed, most collected, most revered wine in the world. 1.8 hectares, ~6,000 bottles per year — this is the distillation of Burgundy. It is not just wine; it is art, history, culture, and terroir. Price: €20,000–30,000/bottle (2026 market). Is it worth it? That question misses the point.
lessons.3.slides.4.title: The Tasting Note Progression Path
lessons.3.slides.4.content: **Stage 1 — Beginner (0–1 yr)**: Focus: learning basic vocabulary; typical notes: 'smells like cherries, smooth'; goals: master the 20 basic tasting terms; tools: take a formal tasting course; target: 50–100 wines. **Stage 2 — Advanced (1–3 yrs)**: Focus: systematic tasting notes; typical notes: using WSET structure; goals: identify primary/secondary/tertiary aromas; master scoring; tools: attend comparative tastings; target: 200–500 wines. **Stage 3 — Professional (3–5 yrs)**: Focus: blind tasting ability; typical notes: full professional notes in 5 minutes; goals: blind tasting ID at appellation level; build personal scoring style; tools: group blind tastings, study producers in-depth; target: 500–1000 wines. **Stage 4 — Expert (5+ yrs)**: Focus: depth and nuance; typical notes: capturing terroir nuances, tracking a wine's evolution; goals: identify specific Grand Cru plots, producer style recognition; contribute tasting notes to professional platforms; tools: vertical tastings, cellar management; target: 1000+ wines. **The Most Important Principle**: Quantity leads to quality. Every tasting adds to your sensory memory. Never stop writing notes — even 3 lines are better than nothing. Build your own personal flavour library.
lessons.3.slides.5.title: Three Levels of Tasting Note Comparison
lessons.3.slides.6.title: 💡 Building Your Tasting Note Habit
lessons.3.slides.6.points.0: Set a schedule: at least 2–3 wines per week; make tasting notes compulsory
lessons.3.slides.6.points.1: Choose a system: CellarTracker, Vivino, or a notebook — pick one and stick to it
lessons.3.slides.6.points.2: Always photograph the label: match future notes to the same wine easily
lessons.3.slides.6.points.3: Revisit old wines: open the same wine 1–2 years later; compare notes
lessons.3.slides.6.points.4: Attend group tastings: compare your notes with others; discover blind spots
lessons.3.slides.6.points.5: Read professional notes: study how Burghound, JR, and Vinous write
lessons.3.slides.6.points.6: Practise blind tasting: buy 6 bottles, wrap them, pour and evaluate
lessons.3.slides.6.points.7: Review annually: look back at predictions; track improvements
lessons.3.slides.6.points.8: Target 200 notes in year one — that is when the vocabulary starts to flow naturally
lessons.3.slides.7.title: 🎓 From Tasting Notes to Professional Expertise
lessons.3.slides.7.content: **Tasting notes are the foundation of all professional wine knowledge** — Critics like Allen Meadows have written tens of thousands of Burgundy notes over 25 years; Jancis Robinson has published more than 100,000 notes; your personal tasting archive is a unique, irreplaceable asset. **The Real Purpose of Tasting Notes**: Record your sensory memory (flavour memories fade — notes persist); track wine evolution (see how the same wine develops); build pattern recognition (after 500 notes, Chambolle instantly feels different from Gevrey); support investment decisions (your notes + market data = better buying); share knowledge (contribute to CellarTracker, educate friends). **Set Your Goals**: Year 1: master vocabulary and WSET structure; Year 2: identify variety and region blind; Year 3: identify producer and vintage style; Year 5+: write notes that are as valuable as professional critics'. **The Ultimate Goal**: One day, you will open a glass of wine, write three precise paragraphs, and someone will read them and say: 'I want to drink that.' That is the power of professional tasting notes.
